fallible

FAL-uh-bul · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Fallible is capable of making mistakes or being wrong; liable to error.

The new intern was relieved when her supervisor admitted that even after twenty years in the lab, he was still fallible enough to mislabel a sample now and then.

Worked Example

Because eyewitness memory is famously fallible, courts now treat a single witness's account with far more caution than they once did.

Fallible simply acknowledges that a person, system, or piece of evidence can be wrong -- not because of carelessness necessarily, just because perfection isn't guaranteed.

Your Turn

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

imperfect: Imperfect means having flaws or falling short of an ideal -- an imperfect plan or an imperfect draft has weaknesses built into it. Fallible is specifically about error: a fallible person or system may usually work flawlessly, yet can still get something wrong.

error-prone: Error-prone means likely to make mistakes, and often -- an error-prone process needs constant double-checking because slips keep happening. Fallible is a milder claim: it says only that a mistake is possible, not that mistakes come frequently.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

infallible: incapable of being wrong; never failing

reliable: able to be counted on to get things right

Where it sits · how often it can go wrong — imprecise → fallible → unreliable

imprecise vs. fallible: Imprecise is weaker than fallible: imprecise work is merely a little off -- slightly inexact -- while a fallible person or system can make an outright mistake.

unreliable vs. fallible: Unreliable goes further than fallible, suggesting frequent or serious failures rather than the occasional honest mistake.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — fall-

root — fall-: to deceive, to be wrong, to fail (Latin fallere)

suffix — -ible

suffix — -ible: able to be; liable to (Latin -ibilis)

Put it together

Put it together: Fallible comes from Latin fallere ('to deceive, to fail'), the same root behind fallacy, which you already met in Part 1 of this course. Notice the spelling: fall- looks like the everyday word fall, but here it takes -ible, not -able -- one of this unit's spelling exceptions.

Use the root in a new word: fallacy

Use the root in a new word: fallacy: The idea that lightning never strikes the same place twice is a common fallacy.
